newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX poised for fresh records, autos lead.
newsitem.headline: German DAX poised for fresh records, autos lead.

text.p: Fresh demand for car shares and delight at Wall Street's strong gains on Friday were set to push the German DAX index to fresh record highs on Monday, dealers said.
In pre-bourse electronic trade, the IBIS DAX was up 33.20 points, or nearly one percent, at 3,524.28, having soared past its old record high of 3,504.27 points minutes after opening.
On the DAX index, which ended Friday at 3,460.37 points before a Wall Street-led surge in afternoon electronic trade, the old all-time high is 3,474.98 points.
June DTB DAX futures were up 32.5 points at 3,538.5.
Dollar-sensitive car shares led the advance, with Volkswagen AG up 3.7 percent at 1,201 marks in early trade and Daimler-Benz AG up 2.2 percent at 137.30 marks.
Bank shares were also firmly ahead, with Deutsche Bank AG up 1.6 percent at 93.60 marks.
"Things are fairly much booming," said a Frankfurt dealer, who warned, however, that turnover was likely to be thin because of the U.K. market holiday today.
"But we can be very happy if we close above 3,500 (DAX points)," he said.

The underperformer of the day was software company SAP AG four percent to 314 marks after Frankfurt prosecutors said they were probing a potentially serious insider trading case involving the company.
Dealers downplayed the move, noting that SAP is notoriously volatile.
"This (the story) is mainly a negative from a sentiment point of view," said a dealer. "It makes no difference to fundamentals."
Chemicals giant Hoechst was also under pressure.
The stock was down 10 pfennigs at 66.70 marks after releasing slightly worse than expected first quarter earnings.
Hoechst had reported pretax profit of 831 million marks, up nine percent when adjusted for special factors.
One dealer noted that some estimates had forecast a pretax profit figure of well above one billion marks for the company.

"Overall the numbers were slightly disappointing," said Christian Faitz, chemicals analyst at Trinkaus Capital Management, who noted that the data had been hard to predict because of Hoechst's current phase of restructuring.
